propositions.text: International organizations operate on sovereign states' territories and need privileges and immunities to avoid undue interference.
propositions.quote: International organizations are active and necessary actors on the international stage. Although they are subjects of international law, they have to operate on the territories of sovereign states with political and legal systems of their own. To avoid undue interference in the operations of an international organization, the treaty that establishes it will recognize certain privileges and immunities.

propositions.text: Immunity from legal process in domestic courts is critical and commonly granted to international organizations.
propositions.quote: some form of immunity from legal process in domestic courts is critical, and commonly granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states international organizations need privileges and immunities to avoid interference and commonly receive immunity from domestic legal process.

propositions.text: The appellant sued NAFO for breach of employment contract in Nova Scotia Supreme Court; NAFO claimed immunity.
propositions.quote: The appellant sued NAFO for breach of his contract of employment in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, as NAFO is headquartered in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. NAFO successfully claimed immunity from this action.

propositions.text: Nova Scotia Court of Appeal held NAFO entitled to immunity under s. 3(1) of NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal held that NAFO was entitled to immunity in this matter by virtue of s. 3(1) of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization Privileges and Immunities Order, SOR/80-64 (“NAFO Immunity Order”).

propositions.text: Court concludes NAFO is entitled to immunity and appeal fails on that point but allows appeal in part regarding separation indemnity payment, with costs to appellant.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I conclude that NAFO is entitled to immunity and that the appeal must fail in this respect, but must be allowed in part, in respect of the right to the separation indemnity payment granted in accordance with the NAFO Staff Rules, with costs to the appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appellant sued NAFO, which claimed immunity; the Court of Appeal upheld immunity; this court agrees on immunity but allows appeal in part on indemnity.

propositions.text: NAFO founded in 1979 as successor to International Commission of Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, focused on fisheries science and management.
propositions.quote: NAFO, which was founded in 1979 as a successor to the International Commission of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, is an intergovernmental body concerned with fisheries science and management.

propositions.text: Article II(1) of Convention states NAFO's objective is optimum utilization, rational management and conservation of Northwest Atlantic fishery resources.
propositions.quote: As stated in art. II(1) of the Convention on Future Multilateral Cooperation in the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries, Can. T.S. 1979 No. 11 (“Convention”), its overall objective is “to contribute through consultation and cooperation to the optimum utilization, rational management and conservation of the fishery resources” of the Northwest Atlantic.

propositions.text: Canada is a contracting party to the Convention.
propositions.quote: Canada is a contracting party to the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court states NAFO was founded in 1979 to manage Northwest Atlantic fisheries; Canada is a party to the Convention defining NAFO's objectives.

propositions.text: NAFO consists of four bodies: General Council, Scientific Council, Fisheries Commission, and Secretariat, with functions detailed in the Convention.
propositions.quote: NAFO consists of four bodies: the General Council, the Scientific Council, the Fisheries Commission, and the Secretariat. The functions of these bodies are detailed in the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court states NAFO has four bodies with functions detailed in the Convention.

propositions.text: Article II(4) of Convention locates NAFO headquarters in Dartmouth and grants NAFO legal personality and immunities.
propositions.quote: Article II(4) of the Convention provides that NAFO’s headquarters is to be located in Dartmouth. The Convention also provides that NAFO has legal personality. As a corollary to this legal personality, the organization enjoys certain immunities and privileges.

propositions.text: Article II(3) requires NAFO and Canada to agree on immunities and privileges, resulting in the NAFO Immunity Order made in 1980.
propositions.quote: The Convention provides in art. II(3) that NAFO and Canada are to agree on what those immunities and privileges will be in Canada. The resulting agreement is set out in the NAFO Immunity Order, which was made by the Governor in Council on January 11, 1980.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Convention locates NAFO's headquarters in Dartmouth, grants legal personality and immunities, and led to the NAFO Immunity Order.

propositions.text: Appellant joined NAFO in 1988 as Assistant Executive Secretary, later Deputy Executive Secretary, a senior Secretariat position.
propositions.quote: The appellant joined NAFO in 1988 as Assistant Executive Secretary (the position’s title was later changed to Deputy Executive Secretary); his position was a senior one within the Secretariat.

propositions.text: Appellant's responsibilities included supervising staff, acting for Executive Secretary, advising Scientific Council, liaising with bodies, managing scientific info and publications, and computer systems.
propositions.quote: His responsibilities included directly supervising four of the Secretariat’s eleven staff members; assuming the duties of the Executive Secretary as needed; providing operational and advisory services to the Scientific Council; liaising with chairpersons within NAFO and the administrators of national and international bodies to fulfill the needs of the Scientific Council; managing scientific information and NAFO’s biological and statistical databases; managing and editing NAFO’s scientific and statistical publications; and managing computer systems as necessary for NAFO’s operations.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the appellant's senior role and extensive responsibilities at NAFO.

propositions.text: Appellant was dismissed by Executive Secretary on June 24, 2005; their working relationship had deteriorated.
propositions.quote: The appellant was dismissed from his employment by the Executive Secretary on June 24, 2005. As can be seen from the statement of claim, the working relationship between the appellant and this Executive Secretary, who had been appointed in January 2003, had been deteriorating.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant was dismissed in 2005 after a deteriorating relationship with the Executive Secretary.

propositions.text: On dismissal day, appellant was informed he would receive $153,149 comprising salary, leave, separation indemnity, and a gratuitous payment.
propositions.quote: On the day of his dismissal, the appellant was informed by letter that he would receive a sum of $153,149. That sum comprised two amounts. The first amount of $102,193 represented his salary up to July 31, 2005, his leave entitlement and the separation indemnity due to him under rule 10.4 of the NAFO Staff Rules. The second amount of $50,956, provided on a gratuitous basis, was intended to compensate the appellant for any financial disadvantages that might result from the termination of his employment.

propositions.text: Appellant agreed separation indemnity of $80,987 would be paid in two instalments; requested confirmation that gratuitous payment was without prejudice; NAFO did not respond.
propositions.quote: The appellant agreed with NAFO that the separation indemnity in the amount of $80,987 would be paid in a first instalment of $30,987 in 2005 and a second instalment of $50,000 in 2006. The appellant also requested confirmation from NAFO that the gratuitous payment of $50,956 would be paid without prejudice. NAFO did not respond to this request.

paragraphs.summary: The court details the dismissal payment amounts, instalment agreement, and appellant's request for payment confirmation ignored by NAFO.

propositions.text: NAFO paid salary, leave, and first indemnity instalment in 2005; appellant returned second cheque in 2006 for separation indemnity and gratuitous payment due to lack of confirmation.
propositions.quote: NAFO paid the appellant the amount due for salary, accrued leave and the first instalment of the separation indemnity in 2005. In February 2006, the appellant received a single cheque for both the second instalment of the separation indemnity and the gratuitous payment. Because he had not received confirmation from NAFO that the gratuitous payment was without prejudice, he returned the cheque.

propositions.text: A second cheque was sent in April 2006 and also returned by appellant for same reason.
propositions.quote: A second cheque in the same amount was sent to the appellant in April 2006, and he returned it for the same reason.

paragraphs.summary: The court states NAFO paid initial amounts, but appellant returned two cheques in 2006 due to lack of payment confirmation.

propositions.text: On June 15, 2006, appellant filed statement of claim seeking damages for breach of employment contract and breach of contract for separation indemnity instalments.
propositions.quote: On June 15, 2006, the appellant filed a statement of claim in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court seeking damages for breach of his contract of employment and for breach of the contract under which NAFO was required to pay the separation indemnity in two instalments.

propositions.text: Appellant claimed damages including balance of separation indemnity, salary in lieu of notice, general damages, and punitive or aggravated damages.
propositions.quote: More specifically, the appellant claimed the following damages: the balance of the separation indemnity in the amount of $50,000; salary in lieu of reasonable notice; general damages; and punitive or aggravated damages.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appellant filed a claim for damages including unpaid separation indemnity and other damages.

propositions.text: NAFO claims immunity under NAFO Immunity Order and that Nova Scotia Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction over appellant's claims.
propositions.quote: In its statement of defence, NAFO submits that under the NAFO Immunity Order, it enjoys immunity from the appellant’s claims, and that the Nova Scotia Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction to entertain them.

paragraphs.summary: NAFO argues it has immunity under the NAFO Immunity Order and the court lacks jurisdiction over the appellant's claims.

propositions.text: NAFO sought determination of immunity claim separately from trial; Robertson J. ordered separate determination of immunity defence.
propositions.quote: Robertson J. ordered that NAFO’s defence of immunity be determined separately from the trial of the appellant’s claims.

propositions.text: Proceedings leading to this appeal concerned determination of NAFO's immunity claim.
propositions.quote: The proceedings that led to this appeal concerned the determination of NAFO’s claim of immunity.

paragraphs.summary: The court states NAFO's immunity defence was ordered to be determined separately, leading to this appeal.

propositions.text: Wright J. rejected NAFO's immunity claim, interpreting 'required' as 'necessary' or 'essential'.
propositions.quote: Wright J. rejected NAFO’s claim of immunity. In his view, the word “required” as used in the phrase “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions” in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order means “demand as necessary” or “essential” (para. 56).

propositions.text: Wright J. concluded immunity was not necessary or essential for NAFO to perform its functions.
propositions.quote: Wright J. concluded that immunity was not necessary or essential for that purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Wright J. found NAFO's immunity claim failed because immunity was not necessary or essential for its functions.

propositions.text: Wright J. found NAFO's functions were to contribute to optimum utilization and conservation of Northwest Atlantic fish resources.
propositions.quote: Wright J. found that NAFO’s functions were to “contribute through consultation and cooperation to the optimum utilization, rational management and conservation of the fish resources in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean” (para. 57).

propositions.text: Little factual evidence supported NAFO's argument that court jurisdiction would impermissibly intrude on internal management.
propositions.quote: He held that little factual evidence supported NAFO’s argument that it would be an impermissible intrusion into the organization’s internal management for the court to take jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Factors against immunity: claims relate to private employment contract; limited to monetary damages; no just cause asserted; no interference with internal governance; no Canadian legislation challenged; no sovereign or political issues.
propositions.quote: According to Wright J., the following factors militated against immunity: the appellant’s claims relate to a private contract of employment voluntarily entered into by NAFO; the claims are limited to monetary damages for breach of that contract and NAFO is not asserting just cause; no right to interfere with the internal organization, management or governance of NAFO is being claimed; the appellant is not seeking to subject NAFO to Canadian legislation; and no sovereign, political or security elements arise in this case.

paragraphs.summary: Wright J. found NAFO's functions and little evidence of intrusion; several factors militated against immunity in this employment claim.

propositions.text: Wright J. noted appellant would have no recourse if court lacked jurisdiction, reinforcing denial of immunity.
propositions.quote: Wright J. added that his conclusion that NAFO is not entitled to immunity in this case was reinforced by the fact that if the Canadian court lacked jurisdiction, the appellant would be left with no recourse to pursue his claims.

propositions.text: NAFO Immunity Order should be interpreted consistently with ICCPR right to fair hearing by competent, independent tribunal.
propositions.quote: He said that the NAFO Immunity Order should be interpreted in a way that is consistent with the right of an individual with a legitimate claim to a fair hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law in accordance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 999 U.N.T.S. 171 (“ICCPR”).

paragraphs.summary: Wright J. emphasized appellant's lack of recourse if immunity granted and interpreted immunity order consistent with ICCPR fair hearing rights.

propositions.text: Nova Scotia Court of Appeal held NAFO immune under s. 3(1) of NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S., writing for the court, held that the immunity provided for in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order shielded NAFO from the appellant’s claims.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal adopted a functional approach to immunity granted in NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: In reaching that conclusion, he adopted a functional approach to the immunity granted in the NAFO Immunity Order.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal held NAFO immune under the Immunity Order, adopting a functional approach to immunity.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found Wright J.'s immunity threshold too high, requiring impermissible intrusion or significant interference.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S. said that Wright J. had set the bar for a finding that NAFO is entitled to immunity too high, essentially requiring that the appellant’s suit represent “an impermissible intrusion into NAFO’s internal management”, “NAFO’s official functions [being] significantly impeded”, or “excessive interference or hindrance in [its] actual operations” (para. 27).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal viewed Wright J.'s approach as overly restrictive.
propositions.quote: In MacDonald C.J.N.S.’s view, that approach was overly restrictive.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found Wright J.'s immunity test too restrictive, requiring impermissible intrusion or significant interference.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal relied on Supreme Court decision in Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid for guidance on immunity interpretation.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S. relied on this Court’s decision in Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2005 SCC 30, [2005] 1 S.C.R. 667, for guidance in interpreting the NAFO Immunity Order.

propositions.text: Rationale of necessity and autonomy from parliamentary privilege applies to NAFO immunity to preserve its autonomy as international organization.
propositions.quote: He found that it was appropriate to apply the rationale of necessity and autonomy adopted in the context of parliamentary privilege to the determination of the scope of the immunity granted to NAFO. He reasoned that just as parliamentary immunity exists to preserve Parliament’s autonomy as a legislative and deliberative body, NAFO’s immunity has been granted to preserve its autonomy as an international organization consisting of many nations.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal applied the necessity and autonomy rationale from parliamentary privilege to NAFO immunity to preserve its autonomy.

propositions.text: Three principles from Vaid: immunity rooted in necessity with broad view; necessity means preserving organization's autonomy; closer employee's tasks to core function, more likely immunity needed.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S. drew three guiding principles from Vaid. First, immunity is rooted in “necessity”, and a broad view should be taken of the concept of “necessity”. Second, what is “necessary” is the preservation of the organization’s autonomy to carry out its functions. Third, in the employment context, the closer an aggrieved employee’s tasks come to the organization’s core function, the more likely it is that the organization’s autonomy will be affected and, therefore, the more likely it is that immunity will be required.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal identified three principles from Vaid about immunity's necessity and relation to organizational autonomy and employee tasks.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal concluded Wright J. erred by requiring significant or excessive interference for immunity; declared NAFO immune from suits interfering with its autonomy.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S. concluded that Wright J. had erred in his interpretation of s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order, stating that he “would declare [NAFO to be immune] from any domestic suit that stands to interfere with NAFO’s autonomy in performing its functions” (para. 44). He would not require “significant”, “excessive” or “impermissible” interference (ibid.).

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal concluded Wright J. erred by requiring significant interference; NAFO immune from suits interfering with its autonomy.

propositions.text: MacDonald C.J.N.S. found Wright J. erred in finding NAFO was not challenging the merits of the appellant's case.
propositions.quote: MacDonald C.J.N.S. found that Wright J. had committed a palpable and overriding error in finding that NAFO was not challenging the merits of the appellant’s case.

propositions.text: NAFO asserted just cause in dismissing the appellant, contrary to Wright J.'s conclusion.
propositions.quote: it was clear from the record that NAFO had in fact asserted just cause in dismissing the appellant.

propositions.text: Wright J. relied on NAFO not challenging the merits to conclude appellant's claim was not an impermissible intrusion.
propositions.quote: Wright J. had relied on his conclusion that NAFO was not challenging the merits of the case to conclude that the appellant’s claim did not represent an impermissible intrusion into NAFO’s operations.

paragraphs.summary: MacDonald C.J.N.S. found Wright J. erred by wrongly concluding NAFO did not challenge the merits, affecting intrusion analysis.

propositions.text: MacDonald C.J.N.S. viewed appellant's claims as significant encroachment on NAFO's operations, more than Wright J. did.
propositions.quote: He viewed the claims as a much more significant encroachment on NAFO’s operations than did Wright J.

propositions.text: Wrongful dismissal actions critically review employer-employee relationships and affect NAFO's core operations.
propositions.quote: wrongful dismissal actions by their very nature represent critical and far-reaching reviews of the employer-employee relationship.

propositions.text: Appellant's claims for punitive damages and solicitor-client costs focus on NAFO's alleged misconduct, asking court to review and condemn NAFO's management.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s claims for punitive damages and for solicitor-client costs focused on NAFO’s alleged misconduct.

propositions.text: Court reviewing and condemning NAFO's management would interfere with NAFO's autonomy.
propositions.quote: For the court to do so would amount to interference with NAFO’s autonomy.

paragraphs.summary: MacDonald C.J.N.S. found appellant's claims significantly encroach on NAFO's operations and autonomy.

propositions.text: MacDonald C.J.N.S. acknowledged immunity would leave appellant without remedy but emphasized legislative immunity must be respected.
propositions.quote: a finding that NAFO is entitled to immunity in this case would leave the appellant with no enforceable remedy

propositions.text: Interpreting legislation to reflect treaty values differs from denying immunity where legislation clearly grants it.
propositions.quote: it is one thing to interpret legislation in a manner that reflects the values and principles of international treaties. It is quite another to deny immunity in circumstances where, by legislation, it clearly exists

propositions.text: MacDonald C.J.N.S. concluded NAFO enjoyed immunity from all appellant's claims.
propositions.quote: He therefore concluded that NAFO enjoyed immunity from all the appellant’s claims.

paragraphs.summary: MacDonald C.J.N.S. recognized no remedy but concluded NAFO has immunity under legislation.

propositions.text: Whether immunity granted to NAFO applies, focusing on interpretation of 'to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions' in s. 3(1) of NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: Two issues must be addressed by this Court. The main one is whether the immunity granted to NAFO applies. It raises the question of the interpretation to be given to the words “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions” set out in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order.

paragraphs.summary: The Court must decide if NAFO's immunity applies, interpreting s. 3(1) phrase about extent required for its functions.

propositions.text: If NAFO has immunity, must decide if immunity applies to appellant's claim for separation indemnity under NAFO Staff Rules.
propositions.quote: If the Court concludes that NAFO enjoys immunity from the appellant’s claims, a second issue related specifically to the separation indemnity will have to be resolved

paragraphs.summary: If immunity applies, Court must decide if it covers appellant's separation indemnity claim.

propositions.text: Before interpreting s. 3(1), Court will comment on immunities and privileges granted to international organizations, highlighting differences from state immunities.
propositions.quote: Before addressing the interpretation to be given to s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order, I will make some general comments on immunities and privileges granted to international organizations.

paragraphs.summary: Court will first discuss immunities of international organizations versus states before interpreting s. 3(1).

propositions.text: States enjoy immunity from jurisdiction of other states under customary international law, based on sovereign equality principle.
propositions.quote: According to a general rule of customary international law, states enjoy immunity from the jurisdiction of other states

propositions.text: ICJ held state immunity derives from sovereign equality, a fundamental principle of international legal order.
propositions.quote: state immunity “derives from the principle of sovereign equality of States, which, as Article 2, paragraph 1, of the Charter of the United Nations makes clear, is one of the fundamental principles of the international legal order”

propositions.text: UN Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property (2004) codifies state immunity rules but not yet in force.
propositions.quote: The United Nations Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property (2004) is the first attempt to codify the rules relating to state immunity in a general international convention, but it has not yet entered into force.

paragraphs.summary: Customary international law grants states immunity based on sovereign equality; UN convention codifies but not yet in force.

propositions.text: Canada legislated state immunity via State Immunity Act, granting immunity except in commercial activity proceedings.
propositions.quote: Canada has legislated on state immunity. Parliament has enacted the State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18 , which confers immunity from the jurisdiction of Canadian courts on foreign states, except in proceedings that relate to a “commercial activity”.

propositions.text: Canada adopts restrictive state immunity approach, rejecting absolute immunity historically enjoyed by states.
propositions.quote: Canada has adopted a restrictive approach to state immunity and rejected the absolute approach under which states had historically enjoyed immunity in all circumstances

propositions.text: Kuwait Airways Corp. v. Iraq confirms Canada's restrictive approach to state immunity.
propositions.quote: see also Kuwait Airways Corp. v. Iraq, 2010 SCC 40, [2010] 2 S.C.R. 571.

paragraphs.summary: Canada's State Immunity Act grants immunity except for commercial activities, adopting restrictive approach confirmed in Kuwait Airways case.

propositions.text: No customary international law rule grants immunity to international organizations; their immunities derive from treaties.
propositions.quote: no rule of customary international law confers immunity on them. International organizations derive their existence from treaties, and the same holds true for their rights to immunities

propositions.text: International organizations lack territory and population, making immunity essential for independent functioning.
propositions.quote: Such an organization must operate on the territory of a foreign state and through individuals who have nationality and is therefore vulnerable to interference, since it possesses neither territory nor a population of its own

propositions.text: Immunities and privileges of international organizations arise from international agreements and host state national law.
propositions.quote: Such immunities and privileges are created through a complex interplay of international agreements and the national law of host states.

paragraphs.summary: International organizations' immunities derive from treaties and host state laws, essential due to lack of territory and population.

propositions.text: International organizations vary in size and powers, reflected in source and scope of their immunities and privileges.
propositions.quote: International organizations vary greatly in size, sphere of activities and powers. This is reflected in the source and the scope of their immunities and privileges.

propositions.text: UN and specialized agencies have detailed conventions granting broad immunities and privileges.
propositions.quote: Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations, 1 U.N.T.S. 15, and the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the Specialized Agencies, 33 U.N.T.S. 261, contain detailed provisions conferring broad immunities and privileges

propositions.text: Major international organizations negotiate detailed headquarters agreements with host countries.
propositions.quote: the most important international organizations such as the United Nations and its agencies also negotiate exhaustive and detailed headquarters agreements with host countries

paragraphs.summary: International organizations' immunities vary; UN and agencies have broad immunities via conventions and headquarters agreements.

propositions.text: Smaller international organizations like NAFO must agree with host state on immunities, reflected in NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: In the case of smaller international organizations, each organization must enter into an agreement with the host state regarding the immunities to be enjoyed in that state’s territory. Such is the case for NAFO.

propositions.text: NAFO and Canada reached an agreement on immunities, reflected in NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: NAFO and Canada reached an agreement in this regard, and it is reflected in the NAFO Immunity Order.

paragraphs.summary: NAFO, a smaller organization, agreed with Canada on immunities, reflected in NAFO Immunity Order.

propositions.text: NAFO Immunity Order made under Privileges and Immunities (International Organizations) Act, later replaced by FMIO Act.
propositions.quote: The NAFO Immunity Order is an order made by the Governor in Council pursuant to the Privileges and Immunities (International Organizations) Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-23 (“PIIO Act”). That act was subsequently repealed and replaced by the Foreign Missions and International Organizations Act, S.C. 1991, c. 41 (“FMIO Act ”)

propositions.text: Section 16 of FMIO Act deems regulations/orders under PIIO Act to be under FMIO Act.
propositions.quote: s. 16 of the FMIO Act provides that every regulation and order made under the PIIO Act is deemed to have been made under the FMIO Act.

paragraphs.summary: NAFO Immunity Order was made under PIIO Act, now deemed under FMIO Act by s.16.

propositions.text: Governor in Council's authority to make immunity orders is in s. 5(1)(b) of FMIO Act, granting privileges and immunities per UN Convention Articles II and III.
propositions.quote: The authority of the Governor in Council to make orders in respect of the immunities of international organizations is granted in s. 5(1)(b) of the FMIO Act

paragraphs.summary: Governor in Council may order immunities for international organizations per FMIO Act s.5(1)(b).

propositions.text: Section 3(1) of NAFO Immunity Order grants NAFO legal capacities and privileges/immunities per UN Convention Articles II and III to extent required for its functions.
propositions.quote: Section 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order specifies the scope of NAFO’s immunities: 3. (1) The Organization shall have in Canada the legal capacities of a body corporate and shall, to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions, have the privileges and immunities set forth in Articles II and III of the Convention for the United Nations.

propositions.text: Relevant UN Convention provision is art. II(2), granting UN immunity from all legal process except waiver.
propositions.quote: For the purposes of this appeal, the only relevant provision of the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations is art. II(2), which grants immunity to the United Nations from every form of legal process, except where it has expressly waived its immunity.

paragraphs.summary: NAFO Immunity Order grants legal capacities and immunities per UN Convention art. II(2), granting broad immunity except waiver.

propositions.text: Court must determine meaning of 'to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions' in s. 3(1) of NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: This appeal requires the Court to determine the meaning of the phrase “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions” found in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order.

propositions.text: This is a matter of legal interpretation to establish scope of immunity granted to NAFO.
propositions.quote: In other words, the Court must establish the scope of the immunity granted to NAFO by the Governor in Council. This is a matter of legal interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: Court must interpret phrase in s. 3(1) to determine scope of NAFO's immunity.

propositions.text: Regulations/orders must be interpreted per modern statutory interpretation principles, considering authorizing statute context.
propositions.quote: Regulations and orders in council must be interpreted in accordance with the modern principle of statutory interpretation

propositions.text: Binnie J. in Bristol-Myers Squibb: must consider words granting authority to make regulation along with other interpretive factors.
propositions.quote: it is necessary, in interpreting a regulation, to consider the words granting the authority to make the regulation in question in addition to the other interpretive factors.

propositions.text: Driedger: must read words conferring power in whole context of authorizing statute; statute intent governs regulation intent.
propositions.quote: It is not enough to ascertain the meaning of a regulation when read in light of its own object and the facts surrounding its making; it is also necessary to read the words conferring the power in the whole context of the authorizing statute. The intent of the statute transcends and governs the intent of the regulation.

paragraphs.summary: Regulations must be interpreted per modern principles, considering authorizing statute context and intent.

propositions.text: Phrase in s. 3(1) must be read in entire context, grammatical sense, harmoniously with FMIO Act scheme and Parliament's intent.
propositions.quote: The words “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions” found in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order must therefore be read in their entire context, in their grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with the scheme and object of the FMIO Act, and in light of the grant of authority and the intention of Parliament

paragraphs.summary: Phrase in s. 3(1) must be interpreted contextually, harmonizing with FMIO Act and Parliament's intent.

propositions.text: 'Required' means 'necessary' in ordinary sense; interpretation must align with Canada's international obligations and ICCPR right to fair hearing.
propositions.quote: The appellant contends that the word “required” in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order should be understood in its ordinary and grammatical meaning of “necessary”. He also submits that any interpretation of s. 3(1) must be consistent with Canada’s international obligations, as this Court explained in Baker v. Canada and R. v. Hape.

propositions.text: Intervener Canadian Civil Liberties Association argues interpretation should not violate fundamental access to justice principle.
propositions.quote: The intervener, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, takes a similar view, submitting that the interpretation of the NAFO Immunity Order should not violate the fundamental principle of access to justice.

propositions.text: Respondent argues proper functional interpretation entitles it to immunity from appellant's claims.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that, if a proper functional approach to interpretation is taken, it is entitled to immunity from the appellant’s claims.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant and intervener argue for narrow 'necessary' meaning consistent with rights; respondent argues for functional immunity interpretation.

propositions.text: Interpretation of phrase in s. 3(1) is determinative of appeal disposition.
propositions.quote: I will now turn to the interpretation of the phrase “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions” found in s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order. This issue will be determinative of the disposition of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court states interpretation of s. 3(1) phrase will determine appeal outcome.

propositions.text: 'Required' means 'necessary'; immunity applies only if indispensable to NAFO's functions; employment matters not requiring immunity.
propositions.quote: it is argued that the word “required” can be defined as “necessary”. Wright J. accepted that argument and concluded that the immunity provided for in the NAFO Immunity Order applies only to the extent that it is necessary, indeed indispensible, to NAFO’s performance of its functions. On this basis, since NAFO’s functions relate to the utilization, management and conservation of fisheries resources, the organization does not require immunity in employment-related matters.

propositions.text: Analysis must go beyond 'necessary' definition; other interpretive factors suggest broader meaning of 'required'.
propositions.quote: In my view, the analysis must be taken beyond this admittedly common, although limited, definition of the word “required”. Other interpretive factors are relevant to a determination of the meaning of s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order. These other factors point toward a broader interpretation of the word “required” than the one advanced by the appellant.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues 'required' means 'necessary' limiting immunity; Court finds broader interpretation needed.

propositions.text: A strict interpretation of 'required' would limit NAFO officials' immunities to only those necessary for duties, excluding common immunities like importing furniture duty-free.
propositions.quote: If the word “required” were to be interpreted as meaning “necessary” in the strictest sense, officials working for NAFO would enjoy only such personal immunities and privileges as are required for the performance of their duties.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that a strict interpretation of 'required' would unduly limit NAFO officials' immunities, excluding common immunities like duty-free importation.

propositions.text: The word 'required' in s. 3(1) should not be influenced by its use in s. 3(3) because s. 3(1) concerns NAFO as a corporate entity, s. 3(3) concerns officials.
propositions.quote: The appellant contends that the word “required” in s. 3(1) should not be coloured by the use of the same word in s. 3(3), because the former provision concerns NAFO as a corporate entity, whereas the latter concerns NAFO’s officials.

propositions.text: The Governor in Council is presumed consistent; 'required' must have the same meaning in s. 3(1) and s. 3(3).
propositions.quote: The Governor in Council is presumed to have been consistent in making the NAFO Immunity Order. In this context, the word “required” must be deemed to have the same meaning in s. 3(1) as in s. 3(3).

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues 'required' differs in s. 3(1) and s. 3(3); the court finds the Governor in Council intended consistent meaning in both.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted the FMIO Act to consolidate, modernize immunities, and provide reciprocal immunities to provincial missions abroad.
propositions.quote: In enacting the FMIO Act, Parliament sought to accomplish three things: consolidate the contents of the Diplomatic and Consular Privileges and Immunities Act...

propositions.text: The Honourable Marcel Danis explained that international organizations require privileges and immunities to participate and operate in Canada.
propositions.quote: In referring specifically to international organizations, the Honourable Marcel Danis said the following...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Parliament's FMIO Act objectives and Marcel Danis's statement on international organizations' need for privileges and immunities.

propositions.text: Parliament intended the FMIO Act to modernize immunities and make Canada attractive for international organizations' offices or headquarters.
propositions.quote: Thus, Parliament’s objective in enacting the FMIO Act was, where international organizations are concerned, to modernize the rules respecting the immunities and privileges it could grant them.

propositions.text: A narrow interpretation of s. 3(1) immunity would contradict Parliament’s goals of modernization, flexibility, and respect for international organizations' independence.
propositions.quote: To limit the immunity granted in s. 3(1) as narrowly as the appellant proposes would run counter to Parliament’s objectives of modernization, flexibility and respect for the independence of international organizations hosted by Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament aimed to modernize immunities and that narrow immunity interpretation contradicts these objectives.

propositions.text: Immunity is essential for international organizations to function efficiently, protecting them from host state intrusions.
propositions.quote: It bears repeating at this point that immunity is essential to the efficient functioning of international organizations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds immunity essential for international organizations to function without host state interference.

propositions.text: Interpreting a regulation requires considering the statutory authority granting power to make it, per Bristol-Myers Squibb.
propositions.quote: As I mentioned above, in interpreting a regulation or an order in council, a court must consider... the statutory provision that grants the authority...

propositions.text: Section 5(1)(b) of the FMIO Act authorizes the Governor in Council to grant privileges and immunities to international organizations per the UN Convention.
propositions.quote: Section 5(1)(b) of the FMIO Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make an order providing that an international organization shall... have the privileges and immunities set out in Articles II and III of the Convention...

propositions.text: The FMIO Act grants broad, flexible authority to the Governor in Council to tailor immunities to each international organization’s functions.
propositions.quote: The FMIO Act gives the Governor in Council flexibility to determine the scope of the immunities and privileges to be granted to each international organization on a case-by-case basis.

propositions.text: The Governor in Council must assure the international community Canada respects international organizations' roles and independence.
propositions.quote: The Governor in Council must assure the international community that, as a host, our country will be mindful and respectful of the roles and the institutional independence of international organizations.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the FMIO Act grants broad authority to the Governor in Council to confer immunities consistent with international organizations' functions and independence.

propositions.text: The NAFO Immunity Order grants NAFO legal capacities and privileges/immunities per the UN Convention, limited to what is required for its functions.
propositions.quote: The order sets out a scheme by which Canada confers certain immunities and privileges on NAFO...

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the NAFO Immunity Order's scheme granting NAFO legal capacities and functional immunities.

propositions.text: Section 3(1) grants immunity to NAFO as a corporate entity; sections 3(2)-(4) grant immunities to representatives, officials, and experts.
propositions.quote: Section 3(1) grants immunity to NAFO itself... Sections 3(2) through (4) confer privileges and immunities on certain individuals...

propositions.text: Privileges and immunities granted are those in the UN Convention, limited to what is required for performance of functions.
propositions.quote: The privileges and immunities thus conferred... are granted “to such extent as may be required for the performance of [its/their] functions”.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains NAFO Immunity Order grants immunities to NAFO and associated individuals limited to what is required for their functions.

propositions.text: The Governor in Council granted NAFO functional immunity, not absolute immunity like the UN, to enable performance without undue interference.
propositions.quote: In limiting these immunities and privileges to the extent required for NAFO to perform its functions... the Governor in Council granted NAFO a functional immunity...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds NAFO has functional immunity to perform its functions without undue interference, not absolute immunity.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal used parliamentary privilege and the Vaid decision to interpret NAFO's functional immunity.
propositions.quote: In interpreting this functional immunity, the Court of Appeal drew a parallel with parliamentary privilege and based its analysis on this Court’s decision in Vaid.

propositions.text: Vaid is relevant because both parliamentary privilege and international organization immunity aim to remove subjects from court jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Since the object of parliamentary privilege is the same as that of an immunity conferred on an international organization... Vaid is relevant to the interpretation of s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Court of Appeal relied on parliamentary privilege and Vaid to interpret NAFO's immunity as removing it from court jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Parliamentary privilege is founded on 'necessity' broadly construed, relating to dignity, efficiency, and autonomy of the House.
propositions.quote: In Vaid, Binnie J. said that the foundation of parliamentary privilege is the concept of “necessity”, which is to be broadly construed and is understood to relate to the “dignity and efficiency of the House”: para. 29.

propositions.text: A functional approach applies: only acts necessary for Parliament's business are exempt from court jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: In consequence, a functional approach should be taken in assessing parliamentary privilege: only those acts that are necessary... will be exempt from the jurisdiction of the courts.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Vaid's rule that parliamentary privilege is a functional immunity based on necessity for Parliament's dignity and efficiency.

propositions.text: The same functional approach applies to NAFO's immunity under s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order.
propositions.quote: In my view, this same approach should be taken in determining the scope of the immunity granted to NAFO in the NAFO Immunity Order.

propositions.text: The NAFO Immunity Order's wording shows a functional immunity: 'to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions'.
propositions.quote: The drafters of the NAFO Immunity Order adopted a functional approach to immunity, as can be seen from the very words they chose for s. 3(1): “to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions”.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds NAFO's immunity is functional, as shown by the wording 'to such extent as may be required for the performance of its functions'.

propositions.text: NAFO's autonomy and actions must be shielded from undue interference; necessity and undue interference are case-specific.
propositions.quote: It follows that NAFO’s autonomy to conduct its business and the actions it takes in performing its functions must be shielded from undue interference.

propositions.text: What is necessary or undue interference must be determined case-by-case.
propositions.quote: What is necessary for the performance of NAFO’s functions, or what constitutes undue interference, must be determined on a case-by-case basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes NAFO's autonomy must be protected from undue interference, assessed case-by-case.

propositions.text: Whether management of relationships with senior officials is protected by NAFO's immunity under s. 3(1).
propositions.quote: In this appeal, the Court must determine whether the management of relationships with senior officials should come under the protection of the immunity granted to NAFO.

propositions.text: Immunity from the appellant’s claims is 'required' for NAFO to perform its functions.
propositions.quote: In my view, immunity from the appellant’s claims is “required”, within the meaning of the NAFO Immunity Order, in order for NAFO to perform its functions.

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if immunity covers senior official management and finds immunity is required for NAFO to perform its functions.

propositions.text: Wright J. found hearing appellant’s claims would not impermissibly intrude into NAFO’s internal management.
propositions.quote: Wright J. found that hearing the appellant’s claims would not constitute an impermissible intrusion into NAFO’s internal management.

propositions.text: The court disagrees with Wright J.'s conclusion that hearing claims would not intrude on NAFO’s internal management.
propositions.quote: With respect, I cannot accept that conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Wright J.'s finding that hearing the appellant's claims would not intrude on NAFO's internal management.

propositions.text: Labour relations are important to an organization’s mission, as recognized in Re Canada Labour Code.
propositions.quote: This Court has recognized that labour relations are important to the achievement of an organization’s mission: Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50.

propositions.text: Employment relationships must be considered as a whole and in context for immunity purposes.
propositions.quote: He held that the employment relationship is a “multi-faceted” one that must be considered as a whole and in light of its context: pp. 76 and 80.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Re Canada Labour Code recognizing labour relations' importance and employment relationships' contextual analysis for immunity.

propositions.text: The appellant was Deputy Executive Secretary, second-in-command, responsible for scientific mission aspects.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the appellant was the Deputy Executive Secretary of NAFO, the second-in-command in the Secretariat.

propositions.text: NAFO must manage senior employees to perform functions efficiently; allowing claims would unduly interfere with autonomy.
propositions.quote: NAFO must have the power to manage its employees, especially those in senior positions, if it is to perform its functions efficiently.

propositions.text: Allowing employment claims of senior officials in Canadian courts would interfere with NAFO’s autonomy and managerial operations.
propositions.quote: To allow employment-related claims of senior officials to proceed in Canadian courts would constitute undue interference with NAFO’s autonomy in performing its functions and would amount to submitting its managerial operations to the oversight of its host state’s institutions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds NAFO must manage senior staff without undue interference; allowing claims would interfere with autonomy.

propositions.text: The appellant alleges improper management practices and seeks punitive damages, asking court to judge NAFO’s management.
propositions.quote: In his statement of claim, he alleges that the Executive Secretary “engaged in improper management practices”: A.R., vol. II, at p. 13.

propositions.text: Such judicial scrutiny would interfere with NAFO’s internal management and autonomy.
propositions.quote: That, in my view, would constitute interference with NAFO’s internal management, which goes directly to its autonomy.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant’s claims would interfere with NAFO’s internal management and autonomy by inviting court judgment.

propositions.text: Appellant and intervener argue immunity would deny justice by leaving appellant without forum or remedy.
propositions.quote: Both the appellant and the intervener submit that to find that NAFO is entitled to immunity would constitute a denial of justice, because the appellant would be left without a forum to air his grievances and without a remedy.

propositions.text: Intervener argues absence of dispute resolution at NAFO militates against immunity, relying on Canadian Bill of Rights and European case law.
propositions.quote: The intervener, relying on the Canadian Bill of Rights... and European case law, submits that the absence of a dispute resolution mechanism at NAFO should militate against such a finding.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant and intervener argue immunity denies justice due to no forum; intervener cites Canadian Bill of Rights and European law.

propositions.text: Absence of dispute resolution or internal review is not determinative of immunity entitlement.
propositions.quote: The absence of a dispute resolution mechanism or of an internal review process is not, in and of itself, determinative of whether NAFO is entitled to immunity.

propositions.text: Employment relationships must be considered as a whole and in context for immunity analysis.
propositions.quote: As I mentioned above, an employment relationship must be considered as a whole and in light of its context.

propositions.text: European cases cited arise in different legal context (European Convention on Human Rights).
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the European cases upon which the intervener relies arose in a different legal context, namely that of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, 213 U.N.T.S. 221.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds lack of dispute resolution is not determinative; employment relationships require contextual analysis; European cases differ legally.

propositions.text: Section 2(e) of the Canadian Bill of Rights provides a procedural right to a fair hearing, not a substantive right to make a claim.
propositions.quote: the “right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations” recognized in s. 2(e) does not create a substantive right to make a claim

propositions.text: Islamic Republic of Iran v. Hashemi and Authorson v. Canada confirm s. 2(e) is a procedural right source.
propositions.quote: (See also Islamic Republic of Iran v. Hashemi, 2012 QCCA 1449, [2012] R.J.Q. 1567, at para. 109; Authorson v. Canada (Attorney General), 2003 SCC 39, [2003] 2 S.C.R. 40, at paras. 59-61.) Section 2(e) is the source of a procedural right, not of a substantive right.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 2(e) of the Canadian Bill of Rights grants a procedural right to a fair hearing, not a substantive right to claim.

propositions.text: Article 14 of the ICCPR guarantees a procedural right to a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal.
propositions.quote: art. 14 creates a guarantee of a procedural nature

propositions.text: UN Human Rights Committee commentary states immunity based on international law does not violate art. 14 of ICCPR.
propositions.quote: United Nations Human Rights Committee explains that a limitation on this right that is based on an immunity deriving from international law would not violate art. 14

paragraphs.summary: The court states art. 14 ICCPR guarantees a procedural fair hearing right and immunity under international law does not violate it.

propositions.text: It is unfortunate the appellant has no forum, but immunity inherently shields matters from host state courts.
propositions.quote: it is the nature of an immunity to shield certain matters from the jurisdiction of the host state’s courts

propositions.text: La Forest J. in Re Canada Labour Code said immunity inevitably leaves some parties without legal recourse as a policy choice.
propositions.quote: it is an “inevitable result” of a grant of immunity that certain parties will be left without legal recourse, and this is a “policy choice implicit” in the legislation: p. 91

propositions.text: The same principle of immunity applies in this case as in sovereign immunity context.
propositions.quote: The same holds true in the instant case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds immunity inevitably leaves some without recourse, a policy choice, and applies here as in sovereign immunity.

propositions.text: The appellant claims $50,000 separation indemnity; Court of Appeal held NAFO immune from all claims.
propositions.quote: The appellant also claims the balance of the separation indemnity in the amount of $50,000. Although the Court of Appeal did not address this issue directly, it concluded that NAFO enjoys immunity from all the appellant’s claims

propositions.text: NAFO argues immunity covers the separation indemnity claim linked to management attacks.
propositions.quote: NAFO submits that because the appellant’s statement of claim inextricably links his attacks on its management with its failure to pay the second allotment of the separation indemnity, it enjoys immunity from this claim as well

propositions.text: The court finds NAFO's position on immunity for the separation indemnity claim untenable.
propositions.quote: In my view, this position is untenable

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellant's $50,000 indemnity claim; NAFO claims immunity for it, but the court rejects that position.

propositions.text: The separation indemnity claim relates only to rule 10.4, requiring payment regardless of termination reason.
propositions.quote: this claim relates solely to rule 10.4 of the NAFO Staff Rules, which provides that a separation indemnity must be paid to any departing employee, regardless of the reasons for the termination of the employment relationship

propositions.text: Enforcing rule 10.4 does not subject NAFO's management to Canadian court oversight or interfere with its functions.
propositions.quote: The enforcement of rule 10.4 would not amount to submitting NAFO’s managerial operations to the oversight of Canadian courts. The separation indemnity claim would in no way interfere with NAFO’s performance of its functions

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the indemnity claim concerns rule 10.4 and does not interfere with NAFO's management or functions.

propositions.text: NAFO concedes it owes separation indemnity and that immunity does not cover claims seeking payment under Staff Rules.
propositions.quote: NAFO recognizes that a separation indemnity is owed to the appellant under the Staff Rules and concedes that the “Immunity Order does not immunize NAFO from a lawsuit that only seeks payment of entitlements under the NAFO Staff Rules”

propositions.text: This concession simplifies resolution of the separation indemnity claim issue.
propositions.quote: the resolution of this issue is made even simpler in this case because NAFO recognizes that a separation indemnity is owed to the appellant under the Staff Rules and concedes that the “Immunity Order does not immunize NAFO from a lawsuit that only seeks payment of entitlements under the NAFO Staff Rules”

paragraphs.summary: NAFO admits owing the indemnity and that immunity does not bar such payment claims, simplifying the issue.

propositions.text: No compelling reason exists to apply immunity to the separation indemnity claim; it should proceed.
propositions.quote: no compelling reason exists for finding that s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order applies to the appellant’s claim with respect to the separation indemnity. This claim should be allowed to proceed

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the separation indemnity claim is not immune and should proceed.

propositions.text: NAFO has immunity from appellant’s claims except the separation indemnity claim; appeal allowed in part with costs to appellant.
propositions.quote: I conclude that pursuant to s. 3(1) of the NAFO Immunity Order, NAFO enjoys immunity from the appellant’s claims, with the exception of the claim concerning the separation indemnity. The appeal is therefore allowed in part, with costs to the appellant

propositions.text: The matter is remanded to Nova Scotia Supreme Court for adjudication of the remaining claim.
propositions.quote: The matter is remanded to the Nova Scotia Supreme Court for adjudication of the remaining claim

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant, respondent, and intervener are named.
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: David A. Copp, Halifax. Solicitors for the respondent: Stewart McKelvey, Halifax. Solicitors for the intervener: Borden Ladner Gervais, Toronto

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal in part, grants costs, remands the separation indemnity claim, and names solicitors.
